about.title: East Palo Alto Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: East Palo Alto's mix of warehouses, retail corridors, and logistics operations near US-101 and E Bayshore Road means workers face a range of on-the-job risks, from equipment accidents to injuries suffered while making deliveries through busy intersections. In California, workers' compensation is generally the exclusive path against your employer, no matter who was at fault, which means you typically can't sue your employer directly for a workplace injury. But if a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment manufacturer contributed to what happened, a separate third-party claim may be possible alongside your workers' comp benefits. We handle workplace injury claims and can review your situation to help you understand your options after a workplace injury in East Palo Alto. There's no cost for an initial consultation, and no obligation to move forward. Our goal is simply to help you understand your rights.

whyChoose.title: Why East Palo Alto Workers Choose Us

items.title: We Understand the Exclusive Remedy Rule
items.desc: Because workers' comp is usually your only claim against an employer, it matters to have someone who can spot when a third party, not just the employer, played a role in your injury.

items.title: Third-Party Claims Have Their Own Clock
items.desc: If someone outside your employer contributed to your injury, California generally gives you two years to file that separate claim, so timing matters.

items.title: Retaliation Protections Matter
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report injuries, and we can help you understand those protections if concerns come up.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly if I'm hurt on the job in East Palo Alto?
items.answer: In most cases, no — California's workers' compensation system is the exclusive remedy against your employer regardless of fault. However, if a third party like a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker contributed to your injury, a separate claim against that party may be possible. We can help sort out which path applies to your situation.

items.question: How soon do I need to report a workplace injury?
items.answer: California generally requires you to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days. Reporting promptly helps protect your ability to receive workers' compensation benefits. If you're unsure how to document what happened, we can walk you through it.

items.question: Does East Palo Alto's location near US-101 and busy corridors affect workplace injury claims?
items.answer: Many local workplace injuries happen during deliveries or transport along routes like US-101, E Bayshore Road, and Bay Road, which can involve vehicles owned or operated by companies other than your employer. That opens the door to potential third-party claims in addition to workers' comp. We can help evaluate your specific circumstances.

items.question: What if my employer retaliates after I report an injury?
items.answer: Retaliation for reporting a workplace injury is illegal under California law. If you believe you've faced negative treatment after an injury report, it's worth discussing the details with us — we can review what happened.
